modules.title: Basic Life Support
modules.subtitle: Adult emergencies: a shared response for medicine and dentistry
modules.summary: Prepare a mixed FK–FKG team to recognize an adult collapse, organize a coordinated response, and practise CPR and AED use under instructor supervision.
objectives: Approach a collapsed adult safely and call for help early.
Describe the features of high-quality chest compressions.
Use an AED safely as part of a coordinated team.

lessons.title: Sample lesson: A safe approach and an early call for help
content: This is demonstration text. In the real course, faculty-reviewed lesson notes appear here.

When an adult collapses in a clinic, the first responder checks that the area is safe, assesses the person, and calls for help and an AED without delay. In a dental setting, that may mean stopping treatment, reclining the chair, and clearing instruments from the mouth.
A clear call for help names the location, what happened, and what is needed.
lessons.activity: With a partner from the other faculty, agree who calls for help and who fetches the AED in your clinic.

lessons.title: Sample lesson: High-quality chest compressions
content: This is demonstration text. In the real course, faculty-reviewed lesson notes appear here.

High-quality compressions are delivered in the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum, at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute and a depth of 5 to 6 cm in an adult. Allow the chest to recoil fully after each compression, and keep interruptions short.
Rotate the person compressing about every two minutes, because quality falls as rescuers tire.
lessons.activity: Count aloud for one minute to feel a rate between 100 and 120 per minute.

case.title: Sample case: Collapse in a dental teaching clinic
case.scenario: Fictional scenario. A 58-year-old patient becomes unresponsive in the dental chair during a routine examination. A dental student and a medical student are both nearby. An AED is mounted in the corridor.
tasks: Agree the first three actions and who does each one.
Decide when the AED is applied and who operates it.
Describe what each profession contributes to the response.

preTest.stem: Sample question: What is the recommended chest compression rate for an adult?
preTest.rationale: Adult compressions are delivered at 100 to 120 per minute.

preTest.stem: Sample question: What is the recommended compression depth for an adult?
preTest.rationale: Adult compressions should reach 5 to 6 cm.

preTest.stem: Sample question: An adult collapses in the clinic corridor. What do you check before approaching?

options.text: That the area is safe for you and the patient
Whether the patient has a dental appointment

preTest.rationale: Rescuer and patient safety come first.

postTest.stem: Sample question: Where should the hands be placed for adult chest compressions?

options.text: On the centre of the chest, lower half of the sternum
On the left side of the chest
On the upper third of the sternum

postTest.rationale: Compress on the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum.

postTest.stem: Sample question: What should happen between compressions?

options.text: Keep pressure on the chest to save time
Allow the chest to recoil fully
Check the pulse after each compression

postTest.rationale: Full recoil lets the heart refill between compressions.

postTest.stem: Sample question: The AED advises a shock. What must you do before pressing the shock button?

options.text: Remove the pads and reapply them
Make sure no one is touching the patient

postTest.rationale: Everyone must stand clear so that no one else receives the shock.

modules.title: Interprofessional Management of Maxillofacial Trauma
modules.subtitle: Shared assessment, escalation, and care planning across medicine and dentistry
modules.summary: Work in a mixed FK–FKG team to prioritize a facial-trauma presentation, combine medical and dental findings, and communicate an agreed escalation and follow-up plan.
objectives: Recognize dental injuries that need urgent action.
Link nerve findings to the likely site of a facial injury.
Combine medical and dental findings into one plan.

lessons.title: Sample lesson: Dental injuries in the emergency setting
content: This is demonstration text. In the real course, faculty-reviewed lesson notes appear here.

An avulsed permanent tooth is a time-critical dental emergency. Handle it by the crown, not the root. If it cannot be replanted at once, store it in milk or saline rather than water, and seek dental care urgently.
Avulsed primary (baby) teeth are not replanted.
lessons.activity: List what you would ask a patient or carer about a knocked-out tooth before calling the dental team.

lessons.title: Sample lesson: Nerve findings after facial trauma
content: This is demonstration text. In the real course, faculty-reviewed lesson notes appear here.

Numbness of the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip suggests injury near the infraorbital nerve, as in cheekbone and orbital floor fractures. Numbness of the lower lip and chin suggests involvement of the inferior alveolar nerve in a mandibular fracture.
Double vision, especially on looking up, raises concern about the orbit and needs prompt assessment.
lessons.activity: Sketch the face and mark where you would test sensation, then compare with a colleague from the other faculty.

case.title: Sample case: A cyclist with facial injuries
case.scenario: Fictional scenario. A 24-year-old cyclist falls onto their face. They are alert and talking, with swelling over the left cheek, numbness of the upper lip, and an upper front tooth that has been knocked out and is in their hand.
tasks: List the medical findings and the dental findings separately.
Decide what needs action first, and who leads it.
Agree a plan for the knocked-out tooth and a follow-up.

preTest.stem: Sample question: A permanent tooth is knocked out and cannot be replanted at once. How should it be stored?

options.text: In a dry container on ice

preTest.rationale: Milk (or saline) keeps the root cells alive better than water or dry storage.

preTest.stem: Sample question: Numbness of the lower lip after a jaw injury suggests involvement of which nerve?
preTest.rationale: The inferior alveolar nerve, through its mental branch, supplies the lower lip and chin.

preTest.stem: Sample question: Which finding after a blow to the cheek most suggests orbital involvement?

options.text: A small cut on the lip
A front tooth sensitive to cold

preTest.rationale: Double vision on upward gaze can indicate an orbital floor injury.

postTest.stem: Sample question: How should an avulsed permanent tooth be held?
postTest.rationale: Holding the crown protects the root surface cells needed for reattachment.

postTest.stem: Sample question: Numbness of the cheek and upper lip after a cheekbone injury suggests which nerve is involved?
postTest.rationale: The infraorbital nerve supplies the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip.

postTest.stem: Sample question: Which dental injury needs the most urgent action?

options.text: A tooth that has darkened over months

postTest.rationale: An avulsed permanent tooth has the best outcome when replanted quickly. Primary teeth are not replanted.
